body.text: Indonesia yesterday deployed more than 6,000 security personnel for a trial involving former President Joko “Jokowi” Widodo, amid tensions stemming from the arrest of three senior police officers for allegedly intercepting the current president’s phone conversations.

The three were arrested on Tuesday for allegedly tapping the phones of President Prabowo Subianto and a number of other politicians, journalists, civil society organizations, government officials, and businesspeople. The three were identified as Prabowo’s chief of staff, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, National Police legal division head Inspector General Ahrie Sonta Nasution, and Inspector General Eko Hadi Santoso, a senior instructor at the National Police Education and Training Institute.

The presidential palace has said that it viewed the wiretaps as an “act of treason” that could “endanger state interests and the safety of the nation’s leadership, including the safety of the head of state.”

Asep Safrudin, head of the National Police’s Criminal Investigation Agency, told the press on Tuesday that the three suspects were being investigated for illegally intercepting communications, accessing electronic systems without authorization, and deleting electronic data in a bid to cover their tracks.

He said that the alleged wiretapping took place in 2025 and 2026, when Listyo was serving as chief of the National Police, a position that he held for five years before his appointment as Prabowo’s chief of staff last month.

While the motives of the alleged wiretappers have not been disclosed by investigators, the scandal is an apparent sign of the widening rift between Prabowo and Jokowi. After competing against one another for the presidency in 2014 and 2019, the pair formed an alliance ahead of the 2024 presidential election. In exchange for backing Prabowo’s campaign, the latter appointed Jokowi’s son Gibran Rakabuming Raka as his vice-presidential running mate.
However, there have been persistent rumors of a split between the two leaders during Prabowo’s two years in office, and particularly over the past 15 months.

Listyo previously served as national police chief under Jokowi and is widely seen as a loyalist of the former president, having previously served as the police chief in Jokowi’s hometown of Surakarta.

Jokowi himself has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation, and yesterday’s hearing at East Jakarta District Court was unrelated to the wiretapping scandal. Instead, it is part of a defamation trial stemming from allegations that Jokowi used a fake university diploma before running for office in 2014, which Jokowi denies. As the Associated Press reported, the former president was welcomed outside the court “by hundreds of supporters chanting messages of encouragement.”
Speaking to the press yesterday, police chief Suyudi Ario Seto denied that the wiretapping investigation had anything to do with political rivalries.

“We assure you that this is purely law enforcement and has nothing to do with rivalries or anything else,” police chief Suyudi Ario Seto told reporters. He added that the arrests must serve as a lesson for the police.

But the mass deployment of troops in Jakarta – authorities say they have sent more than 20,000 troops to the capital and deployed some 6,770 police and military personnel to secure Jokowi’s court hearing – is unlikely to tamp down the rumors of political instability at the upper echelons of government.

According to the AP, retired police Gen. Oegroseno, a former deputy national police chief, said in a podcast interview on Wednesday that those investigating the wiretapping of Prabowo and other prominent politicians should “not hesitate to question a former president if necessary.”
He added, “The motive behind the alleged wiretapping operation must be fully uncovered under the leadership of the current police chief.”

There are other signs of a Jokowi-Prabowo rift. Since the wiretapping arrests, Indonesian lawmakers have begun discussions of a possible inquiry into Vice President Gibran’s eligibility to hold office.

Last week, Indonesia’s Supreme Court ruled that a high-school equivalency certificate submitted by Gibran as part of his candidacy in the 2024 election was invalid and had been improperly accepted by election officials. The court ruling did not automatically lead to his removal from office, but Reuters reported that four parliamentary parties, including three that are part of Prabowo’s big-tent coalition, were considering an inquiry into the matter.

“There’s increasingly intensive dialogue in the parliament to invoke their constitutional rights, especially after the wiretapping,” Hasto Kristiyanto, a senior official with the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, told the news agency.

A spokesperson for the Indonesian military said that the deployment of troops into Jakarta was standard procedure. “Troop deployments are a normal occurrence,” the spokesperson said, adding that the military “must always be prepared to protect the entire nation and safeguard the integrity of the Republic of Indonesia.”
